name: Ashpenaz
title: Chief Eunuch under Nebuchadnezzar II
summary: Ashpenaz served as the chief eunuch (Hebrew: rab sārīsīm, literally 'chief of the eunuchs') at the Babylonian court under King Nebuchadnezzar II. He was given the royal commission to select young men of royal and noble Israelite descent for a three-year education in Chaldean literature and language — part of Babylon's systematic assimilation policy toward the elites of conquered peoples. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were among those Ashpenaz chose, and they received new Babylonian names as part of this cultural integration process. When Daniel sought to avoid defiling himself with the king's food and wine, the text says that God caused him to find favor and compassion in the sight of Ashpenaz. Despite his sympathy, Ashpenaz feared the king's anger and referred Daniel to the chief official (hammelṣar). Ashpenaz's role highlights the tension between the exercise of power by the Babylonian empire and God's faithful care for His people amid the trials of exile.
roles: head of the court's training program

keyEvents.title: Selection of Israelite Youths for the Court
keyEvents.description: King Nebuchadnezzar ordered Ashpenaz to select young men of royal and noble Israelite descent. They were to be trained in the language and literature of the Chaldeans through a three-year program before entering the king's service. Among those chosen were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

keyEvents.title: Assignment of Babylonian Names
keyEvents.description: The selected Israelite youths were given new Babylonian names: Daniel was called Belteshazzar, Hananiah became Shadrach, Mishael became Meshach, and Azariah became Abednego. The names included references to Babylonian gods and were part of the cultural assimilation process at the court.

keyEvents.title: God Gives Daniel Favor with Ashpenaz
keyEvents.description: When Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king's food and wine, God caused him to find favor and compassion in the eyes of Ashpenaz. This shows how God directed circumstances for His faithful servants even in the difficult situation of captivity.

keyEvents.title: Ashpenaz's Fear of the King's Reaction
keyEvents.description: Although Ashpenaz showed favor toward Daniel, he expressed fear that the king would react if the Israelite youths appeared weaker than their peers. Daniel therefore turned instead to the overseer (hammelṣar) with his concrete proposal for a trial period.

versions.summary: Ashpenaz was chief of the officials under King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He was given responsibility for selecting promising young men from Judah for training at the Babylonian court, including Daniel and his three friends.
versions.title: Chief of the Babylonian Officials
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Chief of Babylon's Officials' is appropriate, but the Hebrew word used is 'rab sārīsīm' (chief eunuch/head of the officials). A more precise title could be 'Chief Official in Babylon' or 'Head of the Officials in Babylon'.; [minor] The role 'servant' is somewhat imprecise. Ashpenaz was a high-ranking court official, not an ordinary servant. Roles such as 'chief official' or 'court official' would have been more accurate. 'Leader' is acceptable but should be supplemented.; [major] In Daniel 1:7 it is the 'chief of the officials' (who may refer to Ashpenaz) who gives the names, but the Hebrew text actually uses the expression 'sar hassārīsīm' in verse 3 and 'rab hassārīsīm' for Ashpenaz. However, in verse 7 it is possible that a subordinate gave the names. The text says that the 'chief steward' (sar hassārīsīm) gave them names, and this may refer to Ashpenaz himself, but there is some textual uncertainty. Nevertheless, the description is reasonable based on the common reading.; [minor] The account of Ashpenaz's fear correctly refers to Daniel 1:10. The description is good and accurate.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a biblical figure like Ashpenaz, there should be footnotes about linguistic, historical, and archaeological details – for example, regarding the title 'rab sārīsīm', the structure of the Babylonian court, and the historical context.

versions.summary: Ashpenaz was the chief eunuch (Hebrew: rab sārīsīm) under King Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. He was tasked with selecting promising young men of royal and noble descent from conquered Judah for three years of training at the Babylonian court. Among those chosen were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The Bible tells us that God caused Daniel to find favor and kindness in Ashpenaz's sight, which proved decisive when Daniel asked not to defile himself with the king's food and wine. Ashpenaz showed sympathy for Daniel's request but feared the king's anger if the Israelite youths appeared weaker than the others. Through Ashpenaz's role, both the Babylonian court's policy of assimilation and God's sovereign care for His people in exile are illustrated.
versions.title: The Highest Official in Babylon
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Chief Eunuch of Babylon' is accurate and descriptive, but could be nuanced by including the more specific title used in the original text. 'Chief Eunuch' remains a well-established rendering.; [minor] The roles 'chief official', 'eunuch', and 'leader' overlap somewhat. 'Chief official' and 'eunuch' describe essentially the same position. Consider replacing them with more distinct roles, such as 'chief eunuch' and 'head of the court training program'.; [major] In Daniel 1:7 it is 'the chief official' (or 'overseer of the eunuchs') who gives the new names, not necessarily Ashpenaz directly. The text states that 'the chief official gave them names' (Hebrew: sar hassārīsīm in v.3 vs. sar hassārīsīm in v.7 can be understood differently depending on translation). Many translations identify the name-giver in v.7 with Ashpenaz, but the original text uses a title that could refer either to Ashpenaz or to a subordinate. The description should be slightly nuanced.; [minor] The description is good, but it may be clarified that the Hebrew text in Dan 1:10-11 distinguishes between Ashpenaz (rab sārīsīm) and the overseer (hammelṣar) whom Daniel then addresses. This distinction is important for understanding the narrative development.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew expression 'rab sārīsīm' (רַב סָרִיסִים) used for Ashpenaz literally means 'chief of the eunuchs' or 'highest official.' The word 'sārīs' could originally mean eunuch, but over time came to be used more generally for court officials, regardless of physical condition.

The name Ashpenaz is likely of Persian or Babylonian origin. Its exact etymology is debated among scholars, but it may relate to Akkadian or Old Iranian words. Some scholars have suggested a connection to the Akkadian 'ašpu' (magician/wise man), though this remains uncertain.

The Babylonian court under Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 605–562 BCE) was known for its practice of integrating elites from conquered peoples into the court system. This practice of educating young nobles from conquered nations is confirmed in Assyrian and Babylonian sources and was a deliberate strategy to secure loyalty from vassal states.

The practice of giving conquered peoples new names referencing Babylonian gods (such as Bel, Marduk, Nabu, and Aku) was part of a cultural assimilation process. The name changes from Hebrew theophoric names (containing references to Israel's God) to Babylonian divine names were a symbolic expression of shifting power and religious supremacy.

In rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 93b), it is discussed whether Daniel and his friends were actually made eunuchs at the court, fulfilling the prophecy in Isaiah 39:7. The fact that Ashpenaz held the title 'chief of the eunuchs' has been used as support for this interpretation.

Archaeological finds from the Neo-Babylonian Empire, including administrative tablets from Babylon, confirm the existence of a complex court bureaucracy with various ranks among court officials. Although Ashpenaz is not identified in extra-biblical sources, his title and function fit well within the picture revealed by the cuneiform tablets from that period.
